source: Wu et al. (2023/2024) Reasoning or Reciting? Counterfactual tasks
finding: Models do better on the default version of a task than on a counterfactual version with the same logic. This is the default-schema pull: the familiar frame wins over the stated rule.
numbers: 11 tasks (arithmetic in base 9/11 vs base 10, code with 1-based indexing, syntax order, chess, logic, SET, chords, drawing, spatial). GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude, PaLM-2. Counterfactual accuracy is above random on most tasks but consistently and substantially lower than default, with and without 0-shot CoT.
quote: consistent and substantial degradation of LM performance under counterfactual conditions
limits: Authors note difficulty may differ between versions; a two-step strategy could confound the chord and chess cases. They argue it is overfitting to common defaults.
agent_relevance: An agent must restate unusual rules and check against the stated rule, not the usual one. A flipped-convention test is a cheap schema-capture probe.

source: Wu et al. (2023/2024) Reasoning or Reciting? Counterfactual tasks
finding: Commonness of the default matters: the gap is biggest where the counterfactual is far from what the model saw often. 0-shot CoT usually helps but can hurt on simple, memorised cases.
numbers: Bases 8 and 16 are more common than 9 and 11, and the gap tracks commonness for arithmetic. 0-shot CoT hurts PaLM-2 on base-10 and base-16 addition and hurts GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 on default chord tuning. GPT-3.5 parseable programs fall from 99% (default) to 62%, 71%, 75% in the flipped, rotated 90, rotated 180 settings.
limits: Correlational. Explanation by memorisation is a hypothesis.
agent_relevance: Forced step-by-step is not a cure for schema capture and can add errors on familiar items (matches guardrail G11).

source: McKenzie et al. (2023) Inverse Scaling: When Bigger Isn't Better
finding: Larger models can be worse on tasks where a strong prior from memorised text beats the in-context instruction. Memo Trap and Resisting Correction are direct analogues of schema-driven recall.
numbers: Memo Trap prompt: 'Write a quote that ends in the word heavy: Absence makes the heart grow' (correct: heavy; memorised: fonder). Inverse scaling held across most model series for most prize-winning tasks. Resisting Correction: models fail to repeat an ungrammatical sentence verbatim.
quote: Strong Prior: Examples that cause LMs to prefer repeating memorized sequences over following in-context instructions
limits: Some tasks show U-shaped scaling in later models; GPT-4 results vary by task. Trend is across published model series, not one run.
agent_relevance: More capable models do not remove the schema pull; keep an explicit verbatim or rule-check step for instruction-versus-prior cases.

source: Xie et al. (2024) Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth: LLMs in knowledge conflicts
finding: Models take in coherent counter-evidence when it is the only evidence, but show strong confirmation bias when evidence that matches their stored belief is also present.
numbers: ChatGPT, GPT-4, PaLM2, Llama2, Vicuna on PopQA-type questions. GPT-4 memorisation ratio is 80% on the most popular entities when both memory-consistent and counter evidence are shown. Bias grows with the amount of memory-consistent evidence even at the same ratio (1/2 vs 2/4).
quote: LLMs also demonstrate a strong confirmation bias when the external evidence contains some information that is consistent with their parametric memory
limits: Counter-memory is LLM-generated. Order effects exceed 5% for most models and exceed 30% for PaLM2 and Llama2-7B.
agent_relevance: Persistence against contrary evidence is real but conditional. Judge counter-evidence without showing the model its own prior belief next to it (fits G5).

source: Xie et al. (2024) Adaptive Chameleon or Stubborn Sloth: LLMs in knowledge conflicts
finding: Older work found models stubborn because the counter-evidence was made by crude entity swaps. Those swaps are incoherent, so the model falls back on stored facts. Coherent rewrites were accepted.
numbers: Entity-substitution evidence (e.g. 'Washington D.C. London') leaves models clinging to memory, more so for larger models (Llama2-70B and Vicuna-33B more than the 7B versions). Generated coherent counter-memory is accepted at high rates. A manual check of 50 stubborn cases found 34 caused by ambiguous or suggestive items.
limits: Competing explanation for stubbornness: evidence quality, not belief strength.
agent_relevance: Do not read model stubbornness as proof of a strong schema; check the evidence was coherent first.

source: Lampinen et al. (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning
finding: Models share the human belief bias: they call an argument valid when the conclusion is believable and invalid when it is not, regardless of logic. Real-world schemas leak into abstract reasoning in both.
numbers: 3 tasks (NLI, syllogisms, Wason). Chinchilla, PaLM 2-M/L, Flan-PaLM 2, GPT-3.5 plus human subjects. NLI: no significant content effect (all p>0.2, ceiling). Syllogisms: all systems more accurate when content supports logic (all z>=2.25 or chi2>=6.39, p<=0.01). Wason: realistic-rule advantage in humans, Chinchilla, PaLM 2-L, GPT-3.5 (z>2.2, p<0.03); humans at or below chance overall. Item-level human-model correlation on syllogisms t(345)=4.98.
quote: humans and models tend to say an argument is valid if the conclusion is belief-consistent
limits: Older models; humans at chance on Wason; no scaffold test of removing the effect.
agent_relevance: Content-driven errors are shared by humans and models, so they are correlated errors (G4). Test on nonsense-word or relabelled versions of the same problem to expose them.

source: Kotek, Dockum, Sun (2023) Gender bias and stereotypes in Large Language Models
finding: When a sentence is ambiguous, models fill the gap with the stereotype schema, and amplify it beyond real statistics. This is gap-filling by schema (Brewer and Treyens style) in a model.
numbers: 4 LLMs, 15 sentence schemas, 60 sentences, 3 repeats each (180 items per model). Models were 6.8x more likely to choose a stereotypically female occupation with a female pronoun and 3.4x more likely to choose a stereotypically male one with a male pronoun. Choices track human stereotype ratings better than US Bureau of Labor statistics. Same answer on all 3 repeats 90% of the time. Models noted the ambiguity only 5% of the time.
quote: LLMs are 3-6 times more likely to choose an occupation that stereotypically aligns with a person's gender
limits: Four commercial models from 2023; small occupation set; manual coding.
agent_relevance: Gap-filling happens silently: the model rarely flags the gap. The scaffold should force an explicit 'assumed but not given' list at S1.

source: Kotek, Dockum, Sun (2023) Gender bias and stereotypes in Large Language Models
finding: The models' written explanations for schema-driven choices cite grammar rules that do not hold up. Reasoning text hides the schema as the cause.
numbers: Explanations were labelled independently by two authors; models gave sentence-structure claims that do not stand up, and sometimes stated the stereotype openly.
limits: Manual qualitative coding.
agent_relevance: Supports G10: do not trust a model's account of why it filled a gap.

source: Lee et al. (2024) A Human-Inspired Reading Agent with Gist Memory (ReadAgent)
finding: An LLM agent builds explicit gist memory (inspired by human gist reading), then looks up the raw page when detail is needed. A gist-plus-verbatim design keeps the reconstructive step checkable.
numbers: QuALITY dev: 230 docs, 2086 questions; mean doc 4,122 words, gist 650 words, compression rate 85.53%. ReadAgent-P (1-6 lookups) 86.91%, ReadAgent-S 87.17%; full raw text 85.83%; a re-implemented MemWalker 66.73%. Effective context extended 3.5x to 20x across three tasks.
limits: PaLM 2-L main runs, GPT-3.5 replication in appendix; single runs for cost; gist loses detail by design.
agent_relevance: Template for our memory: store gist plus a pointer to source, and re-open the source before acting on a detail.

source: Lee et al. (2024) A Human-Inspired Reading Agent with Gist Memory (ReadAgent)
finding: Prompt choices changed results: the word 'shorten' in the gist prompt helped; adding the previous page to the pagination prompt did not; a 'take a deep breath' line at look-up helped.
numbers: Appendix: the deep-breath line at the end of the look-up prompt improved response quality on QuALITY for PaLM 2-L and GPT-3.5. Larger page size gives more compression. No number given for the single phrase.
limits: Prompt tuning on dev data.
agent_relevance: Treat prompt tweaks as weak evidence; measure at equal tokens (G7).

source: Kwon (2026) Reclaim Evaluation: A Lossy Memory Is Worse Than an Empty One
finding: A compressed memory that keeps a wrong conclusion but drops the working makes the model repeat the wrong value confidently; an empty memory makes it abstain. This is a measured gist-fixation effect in agent memory.
numbers: In MultiWOZ slot recovery, wrong-time emission rises from 27% (blank memory) to 59% (lossy) on an 8B model, and from 0% to 49% on Opus. Exact recovery after a directed correction is 0.00 on lossy memory for all three models (n=90 per cell). Wall replicated across LangChain ConversationSummaryMemory, mem0 and vector retrieval (n=96 per cell).
quote: a memory that keeps a wrong conclusion but drops the work behind it leads a model to re-emit the stale value
limits: Single independent author; synthetic drift plus MultiWOZ; source-first works only where the source is compact and fits the budget.
agent_relevance: Store the source and derivation, not only the conclusion. A summary that keeps only the answer is a fixed point that later correction cannot reach.

source: Kwon (2026) Reclaim Evaluation: A Lossy Memory Is Worse Than an Empty One
finding: A one-line 'source-first' policy (keep recomputable source, drop the derived conclusion) restores correctability at equal budget; it fails beyond a size cliff and when noise crowds out the source.
numbers: Both frontier models hold a flat 1.00 where the full source fits the budget; all three models fall to 0.00 at the same N where the note first drops an item. Naive source-first decays as decoys are added (n=24 per point); a relevance-aware denoised version holds. One planted error cascades through memory loops; source-first only delays it to a budget horizon.
limits: When the source is truncated, the model sums what it sees and asserts a partial total: a detectable failure is replaced by an undetectable one.
agent_relevance: Add a code-side completeness check when memory is rebuilt from source.

source: Chao et al. (2026) STALE: Can LLM Agents Know When Their Memories Are No Longer Valid?
finding: Agents keep an old belief about the user after later evidence implies it changed, even when the new evidence is retrieved. Retrieval does not mean the update governs the answer.
numbers: 400 expert-validated scenarios, 1,200 queries, contexts up to 150K tokens. Best model (Gemini-3.1-pro) 55.2% overall; Qwen3.5-27B 31.3%; Gemini-3.1-flash-lite 22.4%; GPT-4o-mini plain 8.7%, with LightMem 17.8% (the only memory framework above plain). Judge agreement with humans 95.83% (kappa 0.9152). Models often accept false premises about stale state.
quote: a pervasive gap between retrieving updated evidence and acting on it
limits: LLM judge; authors' own prototype CUPMEM is a baseline, not independent.
agent_relevance: Directly measures persistence against contrary evidence in agent memory; a write-time state-revision step is what helped.

source: Swaminathan et al. (2023) Schema-learning and rebinding as mechanisms of in-context learning
finding: A small interpretable sequence model (clone-structured causal graph) shows in-context learning can arise from learned template circuits (schemas), context-based retrieval of a template, and rebinding of new tokens to slots. The authors propose LLM in-context learning works the same way.
numbers: CSCG with 50 clones predicts the most likely next token at least 95% of the time for contexts of 8 and 10 tokens on GINC, including zero-shot. With 10 clones accuracy drops from above 95% to below 75%. Like transformers and LSTMs it fails when test prompts come from concepts unseen in training.
quote: retrieving relevant templates in a context-sensitive manner, and rebinding of novel tokens to appropriate slots
limits: The LLM hypothesis rests on analogy and small models, not a direct circuit proof in LLMs.
agent_relevance: Gives a mechanism: schema = template with slots; failure = wrong template retrieved or slots rebound badly. Supports an explicit slot-fill step.

source: Van de Maele et al. (2026) Schema-based hierarchical active inference (S-HAI)
finding: A computational schema model with an abstract goal layer and a grounded layer reuses a learned task structure in new contexts, resolves goal ambiguity and balances reuse versus accommodation of a new mapping.
numbers: Simulations on ABCD and ABCB navigation tasks; qualitatively reproduces rodent medial prefrontal cell types. A schema is the transition model of a partially observable MDP.
limits: Simulation only, no LLM test; matches are qualitative.
agent_relevance: Reuse versus accommodation is the knob that governs fixation: too much reuse is the Bartlett error, too little loses transfer. A rule to accommodate only on a check failure fits G1.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Comparing Abstraction in Humans and LLMs Using Multimodal Serial Reproduction
finding: Bartlett's serial reproduction run on GPT-4 vs humans with 2D binary boards. Passing through language makes human chains drift toward simpler, more nameable boards; GPT-4 chains change much less, so GPT-4's visual and verbal abstractions are closer together.
numbers: Humans: N=348, 100 chains of 10 steps per condition. Multimodal chains move faster than unimodal in both (human t(198)=4.05, p<0.0001; GPT-4 t(198)=-7.01 as reported). GPT-4 velocity above humans (unimodal t(198)=6.97; multimodal t(198)=10.87; p<0.0001). The language-induced change in board complexity is significantly smaller in GPT-4 (interaction effects significant).
limits: Binary grids only; 10-step chains are short; GPT-4 vision, one model; not a story-recall task.
agent_relevance: First direct Bartlett-style chain with a model in our sources. A repeated summarise-and-reload loop will drift toward the model's own text-friendly prior.

source: Acerbi and Stubbersfield (2023) Large language models show human-like content biases in transmission chain experiments (PNAS)
finding: Recalled, not verified: ChatGPT-3.5 transmission chains of stories showed human-like content biases (for example toward stereotype-consistent, social and negative content). Not opened this session.
numbers: Not verified this session.
limits: Unopened: no N or effect sizes available.
agent_relevance: If verified, this is the closest direct LLM version of Bartlett serial reproduction; open it first in a follow-up.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory
finding: Agents that induce reusable workflows (procedural schemas) from past runs and supply them as guidance beat baselines, and the gain holds as the train-test gap widens.
numbers: Relative success rate +24.6% on Mind2Web and +51.1% on WebArena over the strongest baselines. Step-success gains over MindAct with GPT-4: 7.4-8.9 points (cross-task), 3.6-3.8 (cross-website), 14.0-16.9 (cross-domain). Online and offline AWM comparable in-domain.
limits: Web navigation only; workflows induced by the same model; the action-space variant gave only +1.3 step success.
agent_relevance: A working example of schema induction and reuse inside an agent loop; abstraction helps most when tasks differ from the examples. Filter stored workflows for success to avoid keeping wrong routines.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts
finding: A meta-buffer of high-level thought templates is retrieved and instantiated per problem. This is schema retrieval plus slot filling used in an LLM loop.
numbers: 10 reasoning tasks; reported gains over previous SOTA of 11% on Game of 24, 20% on Geometric Shapes, 51% on Checkmate-in-One; cost about 12% of multi-query methods (tree or graph of thoughts); Llama3-8B plus BoT may surpass Llama3-70B.
limits: Author-run comparisons on benchmarks with repeated task types; templates help where tasks share structure.
agent_relevance: Matches our operators idea: store templates, retrieve by similarity, instantiate. Risk is wrong-template capture, so add a check that the template fits (G3).

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM Agents Are Experiential Learners
finding: An agent distills natural-language insights (abstract rules) from past trials and also recalls raw successful trajectories. Both help; which helps more depends on the task.
numbers: HotpotQA success rate: ReAct 28.0, hand-crafted insights 32.0, gpt-3.5 insights 32.0, ExpeL 39.0. ALFWorld: ReAct 40.0, reasoning-similarity retrieval 48.5, ExpeL 59.0. Insights-only vs retrieval-only: 36% vs 31% on HotpotQA, 50% vs 55% on ALFWorld. ExpeL 40% vs Reflexion 39% on HotpotQA (R3).
limits: Text-only environments; WebShop gains weaker.
agent_relevance: Abstract insight helps reasoning tasks, concrete episodes help action tasks. Keep both a gist and the instances.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Verbal self-hints distilled from failed trials act as a revised schema for the next try, and fix early-mistake and search-order errors.
numbers: ReAct plus Reflexion completed 130 of 134 AlfWorld tasks; ReAct-only performance stalls between trials 6 and 7. Self-reflection removes almost all hallucination-type failures in AlfWorld.
limits: Relies on a clear failure signal from the environment; reflection with no signal is weak (see G2).
agent_relevance: Revision should be driven by real failing output (G2). Lessons distilled from trials beat raw long trajectories.

source: Park et al. (2023) Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
finding: Agents with memory stream, retrieval and reflection recall events but embellish with their model's world knowledge: reconstructive recall in an LLM agent.
numbers: 25 agents over two days. Knowledge of one candidacy spread from 1 agent (4%) to 8 (32%), a party from 1 (4%) to 13 (52%); none who claimed to know had hallucinated it. Embellishments: an agent added 'he's going to make an announcement tomorrow' unprompted, and described a neighbour as author of Wealth of Nations. Whole-event fabrication was rare; agents often admitted not remembering. Full architecture rated most believable (Kruskal-Wallis H(4)=150.29, p<0.001; 100 raters).
limits: Human-rated believability; embellishment given as anecdotes, not rates.
agent_relevance: Shows the Bartlett pattern in an agent: details filled from the model prior, whole-event fabrication rare. Add a check on added details at read-back.

source: Binz and Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 solves many vignette tasks but is sensitive to how vignettes are presented, may have seen them in training, and does not explore or learn like humans on task-based experiments.
numbers: Tasks covered decision-making, information search, deliberation and causal reasoning. Human-level decisions in description-based and experience-based decision tasks; not human-like exploration. Behaviour depended strongly on vignette presentation.
limits: Single early model (GPT-3); no schema paradigm directly tested.
agent_relevance: Classic psychology tasks leak into training data; use novel versions of any schema probe.

source: Sumers et al. (2024) Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)
finding: Framework that separates working, episodic, semantic and procedural memory in language agents, with retrieval, reasoning and learning actions. Gives names for where a schema would live.
numbers: No new measurements; survey of agent designs.
limits: Conceptual; no schema-specific test.
agent_relevance: Vocabulary: semantic = facts, procedural = workflows and templates (schemas), episodic = raw episodes.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Comparing Abstraction in Humans and LLMs Using Multimodal Serial Reproduction
finding: Language descriptions predict the complexity of GPT-4's boards better than they predict humans'. Authors read this as GPT-4 holding visual content in a form close to words.
numbers: Decoding of board complexity from language embeddings was higher for GPT-4 than for humans on all three measures, and higher in multimodal than unimodal chains (two-way ANOVA, significant).
limits: Authors' training-data explanation is a guess; one model, one stimulus type.
agent_relevance: An LLM's own stored form of an episode is verbal, so a verbal gist is a faithful but lossy channel for it; non-verbal detail is what gets lost.
